lines.text: Four moments, and the entire rest of this chapter's material never showed you a fifth one — that absence is itself the point worth noticing here.
Every other way two threads touch the same data goes through sharing a reference, protected by the locks and traits covered already, never by handing over ownership outright.
Take a string, capture it into a brand new thread with a move closure, and send that thread off to run.
Once that thread is running, can the code that spawned it still reach the string at all?
No. Moving means exactly what it says — the string's ownership is gone from the spawning side the instant that closure was built.
There's no copy left behind anywhere to fall back on; the new thread is the only place that value exists now.
Here, the new thread computes the moved string's own length and hands that number back through the join handle.
The spawning side never touches the string itself again — only the single number the new thread chose to send back.
Now try the same shape, but borrow the data instead of moving it into that same kind of plain spawn.
The compiler refuses outright, and names the exact reason: the closure might still be running after the function that created it has already ended, so it can't be allowed to only borrow.
Wrap the identical borrow inside a scope instead, one that promises every thread it spawns will finish before the scope itself hands control back.
That promise is what makes the borrow safe this time — nothing spawned inside can ever outlive the data it's looking at.

lines.text: Spawn a task onto an async runtime instead of a plain thread, moving the same string in the same way.
Does this task face the same restriction a plain spawned thread does?

lines.text: Yes, exactly the same restriction, just written on a future instead of a closure.
The runtime is free to hand this task to any worker thread it likes, and that freedom is exactly why the ownership rule can't be relaxed here either.
The runtime decides where this task actually runs, not the code that spawned it — it might stay put, or it might move to a different thread entirely.
That uncertainty is the whole reason the task has to own what it touches, the same way a plain spawned thread does.
Two separate threads each send their own message down the same channel, and one receiving thread picks both of them up.
Sending is the fourth and final way ownership changes hands: the value leaves the sending thread completely, and belongs to whoever calls receive next.
Here's the standard library's own comment, sitting directly above the code that actually implements this channel.
It names its source plainly: this isn't a bespoke design at all, it's a direct port of an existing, independently proven channel crate.
Four places, never more, never fewer: a plain spawn, a scoped spawn, a task spawn, or a send — that's every way ownership ever crosses a thread boundary.
Two of them demand ownership outright, one trades that for a promise to finish in time, and the channel underneath all of them was borrowed from somewhere else entirely.
